title: 04. Caching: Cache Avalanche
summary: Cache avalanche is the failure mode where many cache entries expire at the same instant (or an entire cache node/cluster crashes), causing a sudden massive surge of misses that simultaneously hits the backend database,…
objectives: What is cache avalanche, and how is it different from cache stampede and cache penetration?
Why does TTL jitter prevent cache avalanche, and what is the right jitter range?
What is the "never expire" pattern, and what are its trade-offs?
How does a circuit breaker limit the blast radius of a cache avalanche?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Cache avalanche is the failure mode where **many cache entries expire at the same instant** (or an entire cache node/cluster crashes), causing a sudden massive surge of misses that simultaneously hits the backend database, overwhelming it precisely when the cache was supposed to protect it; unlike a stampede (which is one hot key), avalanche is *many* keys failing at once — typically because they were populated together with the same TTL, or the cache server itself died; mitigations include TTL jitter, never-expire policies with active refresh, RDBMS-backed hot-replica caches, and circuit breakers.

Cache avalanche is the bulk-failure cousin of cache stampede (Topic 12) and cache breakdown (Topic 11). Where a stampede is many concurrent requests for *one* hot key that just expired, avalanche is many concurrent requests for *many* keys that all expired at the same instant — or, in the worst case, the entire cache contents vanishing because the cache server crashed or was restarted. The blast radius is much larger: a stampede takes down one database query path (the hot key's); an avalanche takes down the entire database, because a large fraction of all queries suddenly miss at once. The classic trigger is a batch-write pattern: an application starts up, warms the cache by fetching the top 100,000 product pages with TTL=3600s (1 hour), and at T=3600 all 100,000 keys expire simultaneously. The next request wave sees 100,000 misses and fires 100,000 concurrent DB queries, saturating the database's connection pool, CPU, and disk IOPS within seconds. Real-world: Netflix has documented EVCache avalanches triggered by synchronized TTLs during regional failovers; Amazon's product detail service has been hit by avalanches when a category page refresh repopulated thousands of keys with identical TTLs; Wikipedia has reported similar incidents after deploys that flushed caches.

The **root cause** is **synchronized expiration**: when many keys are written with the same TTL at the same time, they all expire at the same time. This is a natural consequence of cache warming, batch jobs, and deploy-time repopulation — anything that bulk-writes the cache creates a synchronized expiration clock. The database, sized for the steady-state miss rate (typically <1% of QPS), suddenly sees 100x or 1000x its expected load in a few seconds, and either crashes, times out, or degrades into a slow-loris state where queries take seconds instead of milliseconds — which *extends* the cache miss window (because repopulation is slow), which *worsens* the avalanche (a positive feedback loop, like the stampede). The cascade is the same as the stampede: more misses → more DB load → slower repopulation → more misses. The difference is scale: a stampede is one key's worth of concurrent misses; an avalanche is many keys' worth, so the absolute load is much higher. Real-world: LinkedIn has attributed outages to synchronized TTLs from batch-refresh jobs; Uber's pricing cache has experienced avalanches during surge-event boundary times when many geo-keys refreshed simultaneously.

The **first mitigation — TTL jitter** — is the cheapest and most universal: instead of writing TTL=3600, write TTL=3600 + random(0, 600) — a 10% jitter. The randomness spreads the 100,000 synchronized expirations across a 10-minute window, so the database sees ~170 expirations per second (100,000 / 600s) instead of 100,000 at T=3600. The steady-state miss rate becomes a trickle that the database easily absorbs. Jitter is universal (works with any cache, no coordination needed) and zero-cost (no extra latency, no extra memory). The trade-off is that jitter only helps when many keys have the same TTL — it doesn't help when the entire cache crashes (a node failure that loses all keys at once), and it doesn't help when a single hot key is the trigger (that's a stampede, use singleflight). The jitter range should be a meaningful fraction of the TTL (5–20%): too small (1%) and the synchronized peak is still sharp; too large (50%) and the cache's effective TTL is too unpredictable. Real-world: Cloudflare adds 10% jitter to all CDN TTLs; Netflix's EVCache injects jitter into every write; AWS ElastiCache documents the pattern as a best practice.

The **second mitigation — never-expire with active refresh** — eliminates synchronized expiration entirely by removing TTLs from the equation. Keys are written with no TTL (or a very long TTL, e.g., 7 days, as a safety net), and a background job periodically refreshes them before they would otherwise expire. The refresh job runs continuously (or on a cron), iterates over the hot keys (via `OBJECT FREQ` in Redis or access logs), and re-fetches their values from the database, writing them back with a fresh "no-TTL" stamp. The result: keys never actually expire (they're always refreshed in the background), so there are no synchronized expirations and no avalanche. The trade-offs: (1) **Stale data** — the cache always serves the value from the last refresh, which may be seconds or minutes stale; for read-heavy workloads where slight staleness is acceptable (e.g., product catalog, recommendation metadata), this is fine; for write-sensitive workloads (e.g., inventory counts), it's not. (2) **Refresh-job complexity** — the job must know which keys to refresh, handle failures gracefully (skip a key on error, retry later), and avoid overwhelming the database (rate-limit refreshes to e.g. 1000/sec). (3) **Memory pressure** — without TTLs, keys are never evicted by expiration, only by LRU; the cache may grow larger than with TTLs. Real-world: Facebook's TAO cache uses never-expire for graph edges; Redis's `OBJECT FREQ` + LFU eviction supports this pattern; many CDNs use origin-pull-on-stale (a variant).

The **third mitigation — RDBMS-backed hot-replica cache** — addresses the cache-crash case (where the entire cache is lost, not just synchronized TTLs). The pattern: maintain a "fallback" cache (typically a separate Redis cluster or a local in-process cache like Caffeine) that holds the hottest 1% of keys with a long TTL. When the primary cache misses (because it crashed or is repopulating), the application falls back to the secondary cache, which serves the hot keys without hitting the database. The secondary cache has a much smaller footprint (1% of keys = 1% of memory) but absorbs the bulk of the miss traffic (because hot keys account for 80%+ of requests). The trade-off: the secondary cache must be kept in sync with the primary (or at least with the database), and adds operational complexity. An alternative is to make the secondary cache read-through with singleflight (Topic 12), so even if both caches miss, only one request per key hits the database at a time. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache runs multi-region with cross-region replication; if one region's cache crashes, the other region serves the hot keys; many services use a local Caffeine cache as a fallback for the top-1000 hot keys.

The **fourth mitigation — circuit breaker** — is the safety net that prevents a cascade from taking down the entire system. A circuit breaker monitors the database's health (query latency, error rate, connection pool saturation); when the database starts to degrade (e.g., p99 latency exceeds 1s, or error rate exceeds 5%), the circuit breaker "opens" — it stops sending queries to the database and instead returns a fallback response (a stale cached value, a default value, or a 503 with Retry-After). This gives the database time to recover (the load drops to zero while the circuit is open), and after a cooldown period (e.g., 30s), the breaker "half-opens" — it allows a single probe query through; if it succeeds, the breaker "closes" and traffic resumes; if it fails, the breaker reopens for another cooldown. The circuit breaker does not *prevent* the avalanche (it does nothing about synchronized TTLs), but it *limits the blast radius* — instead of a 30-minute outage, you get a 30-second degraded window. The trade-off: the fallback response must be acceptable (serving stale data is usually fine; serving a 503 is acceptable if the client retries gracefully). Real-world: Netflix's Hystrix (now Resilience4j) pioneered this pattern; Envoy, Istio, and Linkerd provide circuit breakers at the service-mesh layer; most cloud databases (AWS RDS, Aurora) have built-in connection-pool circuit breakers.

The **fifth mitigation — pre-warming after deploy** — addresses the cold-start case (when a deploy, flush, or restart empties the cache). After a deploy, the cache is empty, so the first wave of traffic sees 100% misses and hits the database — a cold-start avalanche. Pre-warming proactively populates the cache before traffic arrives: identify the hot keys (via access logs or `OBJECT FREQ`), fetch them from the database in batches (rate-limited to avoid overwhelming the DB during pre-warming), and write them to the cache before cutting traffic over to the new deployment. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache pre-warms after every deploy; most CDN deployments pre-warm the edge POPs for popular content; Stripe's idempotency cache pre-warms on failover. The combined defense in production: TTL jitter (always), never-expire for hot keys (when staleness is acceptable), RDBMS-backed hot-replica (for cache-crash resilience), circuit breaker (as the safety net), and pre-warming (after deploys). The monitoring signature: a sudden drop in cache hit rate (from 99% to <50%) with a spike in database QPS — and if the drop aligns with a deploy or a TTL boundary, it's an avalanche. Real-world: large-scale services (Netflix, Amazon, Twitter) have all five mitigations in place; the cache avalanche is a "solved problem" in the sense that the mitigations are well-known, but it remains a common incident cause because jitter is easy to forget and pre-warming is often skipped under deploy pressure.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Traffic
    participant C as Cache (100k keys)
    participant CB as Circuit Breaker
    participant DB as Database

    Note over T,DB: WITHOUT mitigation (avalanche)
    Note over C: All 100k keys written at T=0 with TTL=3600s
    T->>C: GET K1..K100000 (steady state, all hit)
    Note over C: T=3600 -> ALL 100k keys expire simultaneously
    T->>C: GET K1 -> miss
    T->>C: GET K2 -> miss
    T->>C: GET K100000 -> miss
    C->>DB: 100k concurrent SELECTs
    Note right of DB: connection pool exhausted, CPU 100%, crashes
    DB-->>C: timeouts (slow)
    Note over C: repopulation slow -> more misses -> cascade

    Note over T,DB: WITH TTL jitter (no avalanche)
    Note over C: 100k keys written with TTL=3600+rand(0,600)
    Note over C: expirations spread across 10-minute window
    T->>C: GET K1 -> miss (expired)
    C->>DB: 1 SELECT (rate ~170/sec, DB safe)
    T->>C: GET K2 -> hit (not yet expired)
    Note right of DB: steady ~170 QPS, easily absorbed

    Note over T,DB: WITH circuit breaker (safety net)
    C->>DB: 100k SELECTs (avalanche triggered)
    CB->>CB: detect DB p99 > 1s, OPEN circuit
    CB-->>C: return stale / 503 for 30s
    Note right of DB: load drops to 0, DB recovers
    CB->>CB: 30s later, HALF-OPEN, probe 1 query
    DB-->>CB: success, CLOSE circuit
    Note over T,C: traffic resumes, cache repopulates
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
Cache avalanche (synchronized TTL, no mitigation):

  T=0       App starts, warms cache: 100k keys, all TTL=3600s
  T=0..3600 Steady state: 99% hit rate, DB load ~100 QPS (miss rate)
  T=3600    ALL 100k keys expire simultaneously
  T=3600.01 Next request wave: 100k concurrent misses
            -> 100k concurrent DB SELECTs (connection pool: 500)
            -> 500 queries run, 99,500 queue (10s+ latency)
            -> DB CPU 100%, IOPS saturated
            -> queries time out, cache not repopulated
            -> more misses, more DB load -> cascade
            |
            v
  Outcome: 30-minute outage until cache manually repopulated

With TTL jitter (10% jitter):

  T=0       App warms cache: 100k keys, TTL=3600+rand(0,600)
  T=3600    First key expires (the one with jitter=0)
  T=3600.01 1 miss -> 1 DB SELECT (rate ~1/sec at this moment)
  T=3600..4200 Remaining 99,999 keys expire, spread over 10 min
            -> steady ~170 misses/sec -> DB load ~170 QPS (absorbed)
            |
            v
  Outcome: No avalanche, DB stays healthy, no user impact

With circuit breaker (avalanche still triggers, but contained):

  T=3600    Avalanche triggers, 100k misses
  T=3600.05 DB p99 latency > 1s -> circuit breaker OPENS
  T=3600.05 App returns stale / 503 for all cache misses (no DB hit)
  T=3600.05 DB load drops to 0 -> DB recovers in ~5s
  T=3600.35 Circuit breaker HALF-OPENS, probe 1 query -> success
  T=3600.35 Circuit breaker CLOSES, traffic resumes
  T=3600.35 Cache repopulates over the next 30s (with jitter this time)
            |
            v
  Outcome: 30s degraded window (vs 30min outage), graceful degradation
```

### Walkthrough
1. **Without mitigation (avalanche)**: At T=3600, all 100,000 keys expire simultaneously because they were written at T=0 with identical TTLs. The next request wave sees 100,000 misses and fires 100,000 concurrent database queries. The database's connection pool (500) is exhausted, queries queue with 10s+ latency, and the cache cannot repopulate fast enough — the cascade worsens until the database crashes or is manually restarted.
2. **With TTL jitter**: The 100,000 keys are written with `TTL=3600+rand(0,600)`, so their expirations are spread across a 10-minute window (T=3600 to T=4200). The database sees a steady ~170 misses/sec, which it easily absorbs. No avalanche, no user impact.
3. **With circuit breaker**: The avalanche triggers (no jitter in this scenario), but the circuit breaker detects the database degradation (p99 > 1s) and opens — returning stale or 503 responses for 30s while the database recovers. The outage is contained to a 30s degraded window instead of a 30-minute full outage.
4. **With pre-warming after deploy**: After a deploy that flushes the cache, a background job fetches the hot keys from the database (rate-limited to 1000/sec) and writes them to the cache before traffic arrives. When traffic cuts over, the cache is warm and there is no cold-start avalanche.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- In-process cache with optional TTL jitter and a circuit breaker.
- Bulk-write n_keys with the cache's TTL policy (jittered or uniform).
- Cache avalanche simulation: uniform TTL vs jittered TTL.
- Shows the database query burst that causes avalanches.
- Trim to a 1-second window.
- Open circuit breaker if DB overloaded.
- Circuit breaker: reject if open.
- Cache miss -> simulate DB query (record for stats).

**Defines:** `Cache`, `warm_cache()`, `simulate()`

```python
# Cache avalanche simulation: uniform TTL vs jittered TTL.
# Shows the database query burst that causes avalanches.

import random
import threading
import time
from collections import defaultdict
from typing import Callable

class Cache:
    """In-process cache with optional TTL jitter and a circuit breaker."""

    def __init__(self, ttl: int, jitter: int = 0,
                 cb_threshold: float = 0.5, cb_cooldown: float = 1.0):
        self.ttl = ttl
        self.jitter = jitter
        self._store: dict[str, tuple[object, float]] = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        # Database stats (simulated).
        self.db_qps_window: list[float] = []
        self.db_queries = 0
        self.db_lock = threading.Lock()
        # Circuit breaker state.
        self.cb_threshold = cb_threshold  # max QPS the DB can handle
        self.cb_cooldown = cb_cooldown
        self.cb_open_until = 0.0
        self.cb_stats = {"opened": 0, "rejected": 0}

    def _record_db_query(self) -> None:
        now = time.monotonic()
        with self.db_lock:
            self.db_queries += 1
            self.db_qps_window.append(now)
            # Trim to a 1-second window.
            self.db_qps_window[:] = [t for t in self.db_qps_window
                                     if now - t < 1.0]
            current_qps = len(self.db_qps_window)
        # Open circuit breaker if DB overloaded.
        if current_qps > self.cb_threshold:
            self.cb_open_until = now + self.cb_cooldown
            self.cb_stats["opened"] += 1

    def get(self, key: str, loader: Callable[[], object]) -> object:
        # Circuit breaker: reject if open.
        if time.monotonic() < self.cb_open_until:
            self.cb_stats["rejected"] += 1
            return None  # fallback / degraded response
        now = time.monotonic()
        with self._lock:
            entry = self._store.get(key)
            if entry is not None and now < entry[1]:
                return entry[0]  # cache hit
        # Cache miss -> simulate DB query (record for stats).
        self._record_db_query()
        value = loader()
        ttl = self.ttl + (random.randint(0, self.jitter) if self.jitter else 0)
        with self._lock:
            self._store[key] = (value, time.monotonic() + ttl)
        return value

def warm_cache(cache: Cache, n_keys: int, loader: Callable[[str], object]) -> None:
    """Bulk-write n_keys with the cache's TTL policy (jittered or uniform)."""
    for i in range(n_keys):
        cache.get(f"key:{i}", lambda: loader(f"key:{i}"))

def simulate(label: str, ttl: int, jitter: int, n_keys: int = 1000,
             requests: int = 5000) -> None:
    cache = Cache(ttl=ttl, jitter=jitter, cb_threshold=100.0, cb_cooldown=0.5)

    # Warm the cache at T=0 (simulates deploy/batch write).
    warm_cache(cache, n_keys, lambda k: f"value({k})")
    cache.db_queries = 0  # reset stats after warm-up

    # Simulate steady traffic until just after TTL would expire.
    start = time.monotonic()
    # Sleep until just past the TTL window.
    time.sleep(ttl + (jitter if jitter else 0) + 0.1)
    # Fire a burst of requests (the avalanche trigger).
    for _ in range(requests):
        cache.get(f"key:{random.randint(0, n_keys - 1)}",
                  lambda k="x": f"value({k})")

    print(f"[{label}] ttl={ttl}s jitter={jitter}s")
    print(f"  DB queries during burst: {cache.db_queries}")
    print(f"  Circuit breaker opens:   {cache.cb_stats['opened']}")
    print(f"  Requests rejected:       {cache.cb_stats['rejected']}")
    print(f"  Elapsed:                  {time.monotonic() - start:.2f}s")
    print()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Demo with very short TTLs so the simulation runs in seconds.
    # Real systems use TTL=3600s + jitter=600s.
    print("=== Avalanche simulation (compressed time) ===\n")
    # Without jitter: all keys expire together -> DB burst -> CB opens.
    simulate("NO JITTER (avalanche)", ttl=2, jitter=0, n_keys=200,
             requests=2000)
    # With jitter: expirations spread -> DB load stays low -> CB stays closed.
    simulate("WITH JITTER (safe)",     ttl=2, jitter=2, n_keys=200,
             requests=2000)
    # Without jitter but CB catches the avalanche.
    # (Already shown by the first case: CB opens, requests rejected.)
```

Cache stampede (Topic 12) is when one hot key expires and many concurrent requests for that key hit the database — the difference is the number of keys involved: stampede = 1 key, avalanche = many keys.

quiz.explanation: TTL jitter prevents avalanche by spreading synchronized expirations across a time window. Without jitter, if 100,000 keys are written at T=0 with TTL=3600s, they all expire at T=3600 — a synchronized peak. With jitter, each key gets TTL = base_ttl + random(0, jitter_range), so expirations are spread across [T=3600, T=3600+jitter_range].
